Satire or deepfake? Where the Delhi High Court drew the line A Chief Minister sued over AI-generated videos posted by an opposition party. On 6 November, the court ordered them taken down: political humour is protected, but not at the cost of a person's dignity. What does that mean for AI content in politics? Humour yes; wounds to dignity no 1 Public figures must accept criticism and political humour. Parties remain free to attack government policies and actions. 2 But there's a "thin line". Holding office invites scrutiny; it doesn't strip a person of dignity. 3 Humans stay responsible. AI makes realistic fakes easy; responsibility for making and posting them stays with people. 4 Speed of harm. Fast-spreading content risks irreparable injury, which justified interim relief. Satire "cannot be permitted to create irreparable wound on someone's dignity." Delhi High Court, 6 November 2026 Adv. Ashwani Kumar 03 / 08

1 Would a reasonable viewer know it isn't real? If not, it's closer to deception than satire. 2 Is it clearly labelled as AI-generated or parody, on the content itself? 3 Does it target a policy or the person? Mocking a decision differs from fabricating conduct. 4 Who posted it? An official, verified party account carries more weight, and more responsibility. 5 Would it be acceptable as a cartoon? If only realism makes it hurt, realism is the problem. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 06 / 08

TA K E AWAY Mock the policy. Don't fake the person. Political humour is part of democracy, and courts should protect it. But AI can now put real people into events that never happened. Until the law sets clearer lines, labelling and aiming at policy, not dignity, are the safest guides. Adv.
